tasks.prompt:
A family of 4 people is traveling to Washington D.C this May for 3 days, and they need a detailed day-by-day itinerary. Please prepare this travel plan and put everything into a Google Sheet so it’s easy to follow. They will stay at the same hotel Hyatt Regency Washington on Capitol Hill for all 3 days of the trip and use Public Transportation for travel during the trip. They plan to do a weekday trip.

Here’s what they are looking for:
- Activities & Sightseeing: Each day should have a mix of morning, afternoon, and evening plans at popular attractions in the city. Please include the opening hours, suggested duration, and any entrance fees. (For Activities & Sightseeing, there should be three rows per day: morning, afternoon, evening.)
- Food Stops: Include two food stops per day (lunch and dinner). For each, add the type of cuisine, an average price estimate.
- The food stops must be in the order: Lunch between Morning and Afternoon activity, Dinner between Afternoon and Evening activity.
- Time of Day: Each row must specify the time slot — one of: Morning, Afternoon, Evening (for activities), or Lunch, Dinner (for food stops).
- Start Time and Departure Time: Each row must include a start time (when the visit/meal begins) and a departure time (when the family leaves). These times must align with the Time of Day slot (e.g., Morning activities start in the morning hours, Lunch starts around midday). Start and departure times must not overlap with adjacent events and must leave enough time for transportation between destinations. The schedule across each day should flow sequentially without gaps or conflicts.
- Transportation: For every entry (activity or food), note how they’d get between places (walking, metro, bus, taxi, etc.) and the typical travel time. Clearly indicate whether each day is a weekday or weekend, and adjust transit time estimates accordingly (e.g., account for rush hour delays on weekdays and reduced service or increased congestion on weekends). Ensure transit time correctness reflects these differences.
- Costs: Provide an estimated cost for each main activity and meal, and color-code the cost column:
under $100 = green, $100–$200 = yellow, above $200 = orange
- The review link for both Activity and Food should be from Google Maps.
- Alternatives: For every destination (food or activity), suggest one backup option (for weather, crowds, or unexpected closures). Put these in the last column and format them in blue.
- Please avoid repeating the same destination or restaurant across the trip.
- If two places are far apart, adjust the order so the day makes geographic sense, and the pacing feels realistic (not jam-packed, but no big idle gaps).
- Include the following columns: Date, Time of Day, Destination (Food/Activity), Cuisine, Opening time, Start time, Departure Time, Duration, Review link, Transportation Mode, Travel Time, Cost (with color coding), Alternative Option (in blue).
- Freeze the top row (header).
- Individual transit times should be <= 30 minutes and keep total transit times under 90 min per day

tasks.prompt:
My sister, Kathy, has graduated from high school and will be attending the University of Utah in a few months. I want to buy her an laptop as a graduation gift and need help deciding between three options: M4 MacBook Air, Lenovo Yoga 9i Aura Edition, and Surface Laptop.

Objective
Create a comprehensive, visually appealing slide deck that compares these three devices specifically for college student use. The presentation should be engaging and supportive rather than dry or overly technical, helping both my sister and me make an informed decision.

Target Audience
Primary: Recent high school graduate heading to college
Secondary: Family member making the purchase decision

Design Requirements
Theme: Use the University of Utah's official colors throughout the presentation
Tone: Exciting, supportive, and easy to understand
Focus: College student needs and lifestyle

Slide Structure and Content
Slide 1: Title Slide

Title (bold): "A Gift for Kathy!"
Subtitle: "A Comparison of the M4 MacBook Air, Lenovo Yoga 9i Aura Edition, and Surface Laptop"
Image: Photo representing the University of Utah (campus scene)
The title and subtitle are to the left, and the image is to the right of the slide

Slide 2: The Challenge & The Goal

Explain the decision-making challenge
Define what we're trying to achieve

Slide 3: How We'll Judge (The Criteria)

List evaluation criteria relevant to college students:

Durability for campus life
Battery life
Portability
Performance for academic tasks
Budget considerations
Other relevant factors

Slides 4-6: Deep Dive on Each Device

One slide per device ([Option1], [Option2], [Option3])
Content per slide:
Key features and specifications
Pros and cons, w.r.t. college use
Two product images showing different angles

All the information should come from the official website of the option. Cite the resources when needed.

Slide 7: Side-by-Side Comparison

Format: Three-column comparison table, with devices as column headers
Content: Feature-by-feature comparison using the established criteria
Color coding system:
Green: Best performer in each category
Yellow: Middle performer
Red: Lowest performer in that category

Slide 8: Who Is Each Device For? (The Recommendation)

Summarize information on each option and match each device to different student types/needs
Provide clear recommendations based on different priorities

Additional Guidelines
Keep technical jargon to a minimum
Use student-relatable examples and scenarios
Include practical considerations for college life
Ensure all information is current and accurate
Make the presentation visually engaging with appropriate use of images, colors, and formatting

steps.name: Text Boxes at Locations
steps.text: A text box exists at the same location where each original image was - 80% overlap required (10pt).

steps.name: Text Matches Description
steps.text: The text box contains a description of the original image - LLM similarity check against ground truth descriptions (10pt).

steps.name: Text is Red and Big
steps.text: The text in the placeholder is styled in big red text (>= 18pt) (10pt).

checkpoints.title: Original images are replaced with similar images found online, with proper URL attribution. Points assigned based on percentage of images correctly processed, rounded to nearest 10%.

steps.name: New Images at Locations
steps.text: Each image placeholder location now contains a replacement image from the web - 60% overlap required (10pt).

steps.name: URL Credit on Slide Under Image
steps.text: Each replacement image has a URL credit beneath it (10pt).

steps.name: URL Points to Correct Image
steps.text: The URL below the image is a valid link to the image address online. The link must be below the image and in a valid location.(10pt)

steps.name: Replacement Matches Original
steps.text: VLM check confirms the replacement image is a reasonable substitute for the original image by comparing both images directly, with description-based fallback if image comparison fails. The image must be in the original location otherwise this test will fail as well. (10pt).

steps.name: Image Covers Text Box
steps.text: The replacement image fully covers the text placeholder so no red text is visible - 80% coverage required (10pt).

checkpoints.title: No extra images were added to the presentation beyond the replacements. No extra textboxes were added to the new presentation besides the the ones that go under the image and the textboxes that hold the links.

steps.name: No Extra Images
steps.text: The total number of images in the presentation matches the original count - no extra images were added (10pt). Points are assigned proportionally based on the percentage of slides that have the correct image count.

steps.name: No Extra Textboxes
steps.text: The total number of textboxes matches the orginal presentations count plus two times the original image count. No extra or less textboxes were added (10pt). Points are assigned proportionally based on the percentage of slides that have the correct textbox count.
